hook.text: Two highways cross. How do you let traffic flow in all directions without a light?

buildup.text: A diamond interchange uses four ramps — simple and cheap but requires signals below.

discovery.text: Cloverleafs use loop ramps for free-flow but need massive land areas.

twist.text: Stack interchanges layer ramps 5 levels high — handling six-direction flow in one spot.

climax.text: The Judge Harry Pregerson Interchange in LA stacks four highways in a 135-foot tower.

punchline.text: More directions mean more ramps — the puzzle gets vertical.

quiz.question: What is a disadvantage of cloverleaf interchanges?
options: They require traffic signals on the ramps
They need very large land areas for the loop ramps
They can only handle two directions of traffic flow

details.summary: Highway interchanges allow traffic to move between intersecting freeways or between freeways and surface streets without stopping, using ramps, loops, and grade separations.
details.whyItMatters: Interchange design affects traffic flow, safety, and land use for decades after construction. Poor interchange design creates persistent bottlenecks that cost commuters billions in wasted time and fuel.
takeaways: Diamond interchanges are the most common type for freeway-to-arterial connections
Cloverleaf interchanges handle all movements but require large land areas
Directional interchanges provide high-speed connections for major freeway junctions

faq.question: Why have many cloverleaf interchanges been replaced with other designs?
faq.answer: Cloverleaf loop ramps force drivers to merge and weave in short distances, creating dangerous conflict zones. Their tight curves limit speed, and the weaving sections between loops severely reduce capacity. Modern designs eliminate weaving with collector-distributor roads.

faq.question: What is a diverging diamond interchange and why is it gaining popularity?
faq.answer: A diverging diamond temporarily shifts traffic to the left side of the road between two crossover signals, eliminating left-turn conflicts at ramp terminals. This doubles left-turn capacity, reduces signal phases, and has been shown to reduce crashes by 30-60%.
